front: Microcytic anemia in a 62-year-old man: how do you tell iron deficiency from thalassemia trait and anemia of chronic disease, and what must you look for?
bottom: Ferritin sorts them; find the source of iron loss.

bullets.clue: Low ferritin = iron deficiency; thalassemia trait: Mentzer index <13.
bullets.treat: Oral iron; EGD and colonoscopy in men and postmenopausal women.
bullets.trap: Inflammation raises ferritin: add transferrin saturation.

back: Ferritin sorts them; find the source of iron loss. Key clue: Low ferritin = iron deficiency; thalassemia trait: Mentzer index <13. First-line: Oral iron; EGD and colonoscopy in men and postmenopausal women. Exam trap: Inflammation raises ferritin: add transferrin saturation.
mnemonic: TICS: Thal, Iron, Chronic disease, Sideroblastic

diagram.alt: Microcytic anemia: ferritin below 45 means iron deficiency, so look for GI blood loss; thalassemia trait has a Mentzer index below 13; chronic disease has normal or high ferritin.

source.guideline: AGA Clinical Practice Guidelines on the Gastrointestinal Evaluation of Iron Deficiency Anemia
source.recommendation: AGA 2020: ferritin <45 ng/mL is the preferred diagnostic cutoff; bidirectional endoscopy for asymptomatic postmenopausal women and men with iron deficiency anemia; oral iron first; transferrin saturation helps when inflammation raises ferritin.

front: Macrocytic anemia with paresthesias, ataxia and hypersegmented neutrophils: what is the diagnosis, the confirmatory test, and what must you not give alone?
bottom: B12 deficiency: treat with B12, never folate alone.

bullets.clue: Neuro signs; high methylmalonic acid (MMA) points to B12.
bullets.treat: IM B12 if neuro signs or pernicious anemia.
bullets.trap: Folate alone fixes anemia; nerve damage progresses.

back: B12 deficiency: treat with B12, never folate alone. Key clue: Neuro signs; high methylmalonic acid (MMA) points to B12. First-line: IM B12 if neuro signs or pernicious anemia. Exam trap: Folate alone fixes anemia; nerve damage progresses.

diagram.alt: Macrocytic anemia with neurologic signs: check B12 and methylmalonic acid, treat with B12 first; folate alone worsens nerve damage.

source.guideline: BSH Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of cobalamin and folate disorders
source.recommendation: BSH 2014: serum B12 first-line with MMA/homocysteine to clarify borderline results; anti-intrinsic factor antibody for pernicious anemia; hydroxocobalamin IM for neurologic involvement; folic acid should not be given alone in suspected B12 deficiency.

front: Child with sickle cell disease has a temperature of 38.8 °C: what is the immediate plan, and what prevents infection and crises long term?
bottom: Fever ≥38.5 °C in sickle cell disease is an emergency.

bullets.treat: CBC, culture, prompt parenteral antibiotics; hydroxyurea from 9 months.
bullets.trap: Cough or chest pain: chest X-ray for acute chest syndrome.

back: Fever ≥38.5 °C in sickle cell disease is an emergency. Key clue: Functional asplenia: pneumococcus, encapsulated bacteria. First-line: CBC, culture, prompt parenteral antibiotics; hydroxyurea from 9 months. Exam trap: Cough or chest pain: chest X-ray for acute chest syndrome.

diagram.alt: Sickle cell disease with fever of 38.5 or higher: urgent evaluation, cultures and prompt parenteral antibiotics; penicillin prophylaxis and hydroxyurea prevent complications.

source.guideline: NHLBI Evidence-Based Management of Sickle Cell Disease: Expert Panel Report
source.recommendation: NHLBI 2014: temperature ≥101.3 °F (38.5 °C) requires immediate evaluation with CBC, reticulocyte count and blood culture, and prompt parenteral antibiotics covering S. pneumoniae and gram-negative enteric organisms; hydroxyurea offered to infants ≥9 months with HbSS/HbSβ0; penicillin prophylaxis in young children.

front: Platelets fall 60% five days after starting heparin: what is the diagnosis, how do you estimate probability, and what do you give?
bottom: Suspected HIT: stop all heparin, start a non-heparin anticoagulant.

bullets.clue: Score with the 4Ts; confirm with PF4 immunoassay.
bullets.treat: Argatroban, bivalirudin, fondaparinux or a DOAC.
bullets.trap: Low 4Ts score: don't test or treat empirically.

back: Suspected HIT: stop all heparin, start a non-heparin anticoagulant. Key clue: Score with the 4Ts; confirm with PF4 immunoassay. First-line: Argatroban, bivalirudin, fondaparinux or a DOAC. Exam trap: Low 4Ts score: don't test or treat empirically.

diagram.alt: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia: platelet fall of more than 50 percent at days 5 to 10; use the 4Ts score, stop heparin, give a non-heparin anticoagulant.

source.guideline: ASH 2018 guidelines for management of venous thromboembolism: heparin-induced thrombocytopenia
source.recommendation: ASH 2018 (strong): use the 4Ts score rather than gestalt; avoid HIT lab testing and empiric treatment with a low-probability 4Ts score. Conditional: choose among argatroban, bivalirudin, danaparoid, fondaparinux, DOACs for acute HIT. ISTH 2025 DIC scoring communication (alt link) supports platelets, PT, fibrinogen and D-dimer scoring.

front: Smear shows Auer rods, smudge cells, Reed-Sternberg cells or a Philadelphia chromosome: which disease, and what must not wait for confirmation?
bottom: Match: AML, CLL, Hodgkin lymphoma, CML.

bullets.clue: Auer rods = AML (APL if t(15;17)); smudge cells = CLL.
bullets.treat: Suspected APL: start ATRA now. CML: imatinib.
bullets.trap: APL bleeds from DIC: don't wait for genetics.

back: Match: AML, CLL, Hodgkin lymphoma, CML. Key clue: Auer rods = AML (APL if t(15;17)); smudge cells = CLL. First-line: Suspected APL: start ATRA now. CML: imatinib. Exam trap: APL bleeds from DIC: don't wait for genetics.

diagram.alt: Auer rods point to acute myeloid leukemia and acute promyelocytic leukemia; smudge cells to CLL; Reed-Sternberg cells to Hodgkin lymphoma; Philadelphia chromosome to CML.

source.guideline: ELN recommendations for the management of acute promyelocytic leukemia (2019); ELN 2020 recommendations for CML
source.recommendation: ELN APL 2019: start ATRA immediately at first suspicion of APL, without waiting for genetic confirmation, because of the bleeding/DIC risk. ELN CML 2020: tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy for chronic phase. iwCLL 2018 (doi 10.1182/blood-2017-09-806398) is the CLL reference.

front: Which bleeding history points to von Willebrand disease or a platelet problem versus hemophilia, and which screening tests and levels confirm VWD?
bottom: Mucosal bleeding: VWD; joint bleeds: hemophilia.

bullets.clue: Male, hemarthrosis, prolonged aPTT, normal PT = hemophilia A or B.
bullets.treat: VWD: VWF antigen, activity, factor VIII. Hemophilia: factor assay.
bullets.trap: VWF rises with stress or pregnancy: test when well.

back: Mucosal bleeding: VWD; joint bleeds: hemophilia. Key clue: Male, hemarthrosis, prolonged aPTT, normal PT = hemophilia A or B. First-line: VWD: VWF antigen, activity, factor VIII. Hemophilia: factor assay. Exam trap: VWF rises with stress or pregnancy: test when well.

diagram.alt: Mucosal bleeding such as nosebleeds and heavy periods suggests von Willebrand disease; joint bleeds in a male suggest hemophilia; check VWF antigen and activity.

source.guideline: ASH/ISTH/NHF/WFH 2021 guidelines on the diagnosis of von Willebrand disease
source.recommendation: ASH/ISTH/NHF/WFH 2021: use a structured bleeding assessment tool; VWD diagnosed on low VWF activity (<0.30 IU/mL diagnostic with or without bleeding; 0.30–0.50 with bleeding is called “low VWF”); WFH 2020 (alt link) covers hemophilia A/B diagnosis and factor replacement/emicizumab prophylaxis.

front: Life-threatening bleed on warfarin, dabigatran or apixaban: which reversal agent for each?
bottom: Match the agent to the drug.

bullets.clue: Warfarin: vitamin K + 4F-PCC. Dabigatran: idarucizumab. Heparin: protamine.
bullets.treat: Xa inhibitors: 4F-PCC; andexanet no longer sold in the U.S.
bullets.trap: Reverse major bleeds only; FFP is second-line.

back: Match the agent to the drug. Key clue: Warfarin: vitamin K + 4F-PCC. Dabigatran: idarucizumab. Heparin: protamine. First-line: Xa inhibitors: 4F-PCC; andexanet no longer sold in the U.S. Exam trap: Reverse major bleeds only; FFP is second-line.

diagram.alt: Warfarin is reversed with vitamin K and four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate, dabigatran with idarucizumab, factor Xa inhibitors with prothrombin complex concentrate.

source.guideline: 2020 ACC Expert Consensus Decision Pathway on Management of Bleeding in Patients on Oral Anticoagulants
source.recommendation: ACC 2020 pathway: for major bleeding on warfarin give vitamin K and 4F-PCC (plasma if PCC unavailable); idarucizumab for dabigatran; andexanet alfa or 4F-PCC for factor Xa inhibitors. FDA CBER list: andexanet alfa (Andexxa) permanently discontinued December 2025, so 4F-PCC is the remaining option.

front: Fever, flank pain and red urine minutes into a transfusion: what is the diagnosis and the first action? How do TRALI and TACO differ?
bottom: Acute hemolytic reaction: stop the transfusion now.

bullets.treat: Stop, keep IV open, recheck labels, send DAT.
bullets.trap: TACO: high BNP, diuretics help. TRALI: normal BNP, support only.

back: Acute hemolytic reaction: stop the transfusion now. Key clue: ABO mismatch: fever, hypotension, hemoglobinuria. First-line: Stop, keep IV open, recheck labels, send DAT. Exam trap: TACO: high BNP, diuretics help. TRALI: normal BNP, support only.

diagram.alt: Transfusion reaction with fever, flank pain and dark urine: stop the transfusion, recheck labels, send direct antiglobulin test; TRALI and TACO cause pulmonary edema.

source.guideline: CDC NHSN Hemovigilance Module Protocol (transfusion reaction definitions)
source.recommendation: CDC NHSN hemovigilance definitions: acute hemolytic reaction, TRALI (acute hypoxemia/bilateral infiltrates within 6 h, no left-atrial hypertension) and TACO (circulatory overload within 12 h, elevated BNP). Management steps (stop, recheck, DAT) are standard transfusion-medicine teaching.

front: Older adult with back pain, anemia, rising creatinine and calcium 12 mg/dL: what is the diagnosis and the first tests?

bullets.clue: CRAB: Calcium, Renal failure, Anemia, Bone lesions; rouleaux.
bullets.treat: Serum protein electrophoresis, immunofixation, free light chains, marrow biopsy.
bullets.trap: Dipstick misses light chains: send urine electrophoresis.

back: Multiple myeloma until proven otherwise. Key clue: CRAB: Calcium, Renal failure, Anemia, Bone lesions; rouleaux. First-line: Serum protein electrophoresis, immunofixation, free light chains, marrow biopsy. Exam trap: Dipstick misses light chains: send urine electrophoresis.

diagram.alt: Multiple myeloma: back pain, anemia, kidney injury and high calcium; CRAB features; check serum protein electrophoresis, free light chains and bone marrow.

source.guideline: IMWG updated criteria for the diagnosis of multiple myeloma
source.recommendation: IMWG 2014: clonal marrow plasma cells ≥10% (or biopsy-proven plasmacytoma) plus a myeloma-defining event: CRAB features, or ≥60% marrow plasma cells, serum FLC ratio ≥100 (involved ≥100 mg/L), or >1 focal MRI lesion.
